ai.definition: AI safety focuses on developing methods to ensure that artificial intelligence systems operate in a manner consistent with the intended goals, without causing harm or unintended consequences. This involves addressing ethical issues related to AI's development and deployment.
ai.howItWorks: AI safety mechanisms include transparency about how algorithms work, alignment of AI objectives with human values, and rigorous testing to prevent harmful outcomes. Techniques such as robustness checks, fail-safes, and ethical guidelines are integrated into the design process to ensure that AI systems behave predictably and ethically.
ai.problemSolved: AI safety addresses the risks associated with unintended consequences and unethical behavior in AI systems, ensuring they operate safely and align with societal values.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing processes for AI safety involve developing algorithms, implementing ethical guidelines, and integrating safety features into AI systems. This includes testing and validation to ensure that AI operates as intended without causing harm.
ai.buildProcess: The build process for AI safety involves defining clear objectives, designing algorithms with transparency in mind, incorporating fail-safes, and conducting thorough testing before deployment. Continuous monitoring and updates are necessary to maintain safety standards.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the development of robust ethical guidelines, rigorous testing protocols, and the integration of safety features into AI systems. Ongoing maintenance and updates also contribute to costs.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: AI safety is expected to grow as a critical component in the deployment of AI technologies, with increasing emphasis on ethical considerations and regulatory compliance.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks for AI safety are still evolving but are expected to become more stringent. Compliance with these regulations will be crucial for the adoption and acceptance of AI systems.
ai.risks: Risks include potential unintended consequences, lack of transparency, and failure to align AI objectives with human values. These can lead to ethical violations, legal issues, and loss of public trust.
ai.profitability: Profitability in AI safety is driven by the demand for safe and ethical AI systems from businesses and governments. However, costs associated with development and compliance may initially limit profitability.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments in AI safety will likely focus on enhancing transparency, improving robustness against adversarial attacks, and ensuring alignment with evolving societal values.

glossary.def: Tests to ensure that AI systems behave predictably under various conditions and do not exhibit unexpected behavior.
Mechanisms designed to prevent or mitigate harm in the event of system failure or unintended operation.
Standards and principles that guide the development, deployment, and use of AI systems to ensure they align with societal values.

subsystems.name: Specification and threat modelling
subsystems.role: defines what the system should and should not do, and which failures matter most.

subsystems.name: Alignment training
subsystems.role: shapes the model's behaviour toward the intended policy during training.
parts: policy optimisation (e.g. reinforcement learning from human feedback)

subsystems.name: Evaluation and red-teaming
subsystems.role: tries to make the system fail before release.

subsystems.name: Interpretability
subsystems.role: opens the model's internals to see what features and circuits drive an output.

subsystems.name: Runtime guardrails
subsystems.role: filters and monitors the deployed system.

subsystems.name: Governance and incident response
subsystems.role: makes safety repeatable and auditable across releases.

buildSteps.title: Write the specification
buildSteps.detail: State the intended behaviour, forbidden behaviours and acceptable failure rates in plain, testable terms.

buildSteps.title: Collect demonstration data
buildSteps.detail: People write the responses the model should give, including refusals and safe handling of sensitive requests.

buildSteps.title: Collect preference data
buildSteps.detail: Annotators compare pairs of model outputs and say which is better, turning a vague goal into a ranking signal.

buildSteps.title: Train a reward model and tune the policy
buildSteps.detail: The preference data trains a scorer, and the language model is optimised against it — with a penalty for drifting too far from the original model, which otherwise learns to game the scorer.

buildSteps.title: Red-team and evaluate
buildSteps.detail: Attackers, human and automated, probe for jailbreaks, deception and dangerous capabilities; results are turned into new test cases.

buildSteps.title: Inspect the internals
buildSteps.detail: Interpretability tools map which internal features activate on risky inputs, so a failure can be diagnosed rather than just patched.

buildSteps.title: Shield the deployed system
buildSteps.detail: Wrap the model in input and output classifiers, restrict what tools and data it can reach, and log every interaction.

buildSteps.title: Monitor and retrain
buildSteps.detail: Real-world misuse and errors are fed back into the next training round, and guardrail thresholds are retuned.

prerequisites.why: alignment training needs millions of human comparisons, which is slow, costly and culturally biased.
researchers can identify some features and circuits, but not yet read off a model's intentions reliably.
attack generation scales better than human red teams, but the strongest attacks are still found by people.
a guardrail is useless if it adds more latency or cost than the product can bear.
there is no general method to prove a trained network will never emit a forbidden output.

pathway.milestone: frontier developers run internal pre-deployment evaluations and publish safety frameworks
pathway.unlocks: a common vocabulary of risks, evaluations and mitigations.

pathway.milestone: independent third-party evaluation and standardised safety benchmarks
pathway.unlocks: claims about a model's safety become checkable rather than self-reported.

pathway.milestone: regulation requiring evaluation of high-risk systems before release
pathway.unlocks: safety work becomes a condition of market access, not a voluntary extra.

pathway.milestone: scalable oversight and interpretability that work on systems whose reasoning we cannot fully check
pathway.unlocks: the ability to keep supervising models that are more capable than the people auditing them.
